modules.title: What AI is
modules.desc: What artificial intelligence is, how it learns, and where lawyers already meet it.
recap: AI is software that learns patterns from examples. Nobody writes all its rules by hand.
Courts have accepted some AI for years, such as technology-assisted review in e-discovery.
AI has no duties and cannot be disciplined. The lawyer stays responsible for the work.

scenario.q: Your firm's e-discovery vendor says it "uses AI" to rank documents. Which question best tells you whether you can rely on it?
opts: Is it the newest kind of AI?
How was it trained on this matter, and how was its accuracy checked on a sample of our documents?
Does it use a chatbot?
How much does it cost?
scenario.feedback: What matters is how the tool learned from this matter's documents and how its results were checked. Testing on a sample is how courts and parties judge review tools.

modules.title: Generative AI
modules.desc: AI that drafts, sums up and makes pictures and voices. What it means for evidence, copyright and fraud.
recap: Generative AI makes new text, pictures, sound and video. A fast draft is only useful once someone checks it.
AI can make fake photos, voices and videos that look real. Ask where any file came from before relying on it.
Courts are still deciding who owns AI-made work and what AI may train on. Confirm payment changes by calling a number you already have.

scenario.q: A client sends you a video that appears to show the other driver admitting fault. What do you do before relying on it?
opts: Use it, because videos cannot be faked
Ask a chatbot whether it is real
Ask where it came from, get the original file and its details, and consider an expert if it matters
Post it online to see what people think
scenario.feedback: AI can make realistic fake video. Where the file came from, the original file and, when the stakes are high, an expert are what count.

modules.title: Chatbots and AI models
modules.desc: How chatbots work, how to ask good legal questions, why they invent cases, and how to pick a tool.
recap: A language model writes by guessing the next word, so it can produce cases that sound real but are not.
Good prompts give your role, the place, the task and the format, and leave client details out.
Lawyers have been sanctioned for filing fake AI citations. Read every case you cite.
Legal research tools are better than general chatbots for finding authority, but they still make mistakes.

scenario.q: Late at night, a chatbot gives you three cases that perfectly support a motion due in the morning. What do you do?
opts: File them, because they look right
Ask the chatbot whether the cases are real
Cite them with "see generally"
Find and read each case in a trusted database before citing it, and drop any you cannot find
scenario.feedback: This is how the lawyers in Mata v. Avianca got into trouble. Only reading the case from a trusted source shows that it exists and says what you need.

modules.title: AI in legal work
modules.desc: Using AI for legal writing, for law school and at a legal job, within the rules.
recap: Let AI write a first draft, then check every fact and legal point and rewrite it in your own words.
In law school, follow your school's rules and use AI to test yourself, not to skip the reading.
At work, use only approved tools for client information, bill honestly and supervise others' AI use.

scenario.q: A senior associate asks you to paste a client's draft merger agreement into a free chatbot to sum it up. What do you do?
opts: Use the firm's approved tool for client documents, or remove identifying details, and follow the firm's AI policy
Paste it in, because a senior associate asked
Paste it in and delete the chat afterward
Refuse to help with the summary at all
scenario.feedback: Client documents belong only in tools approved for them. Deleting a chat afterward does not undo sharing it.

modules.title: Fairness, privacy and legal jobs
modules.desc: Bias in AI used for bail, sentencing and hiring, what happens to what you type, and how legal jobs are changing.
recap: AI can repeat unfair patterns. Courts and lawmakers have set limits on tools like risk scores and hiring screens.
AI chats may be saved, read or handed over. A court has held a client's own AI chats were not privileged.
Routine review and drafting are changing most. Judgment, advocacy and client care matter more.

scenario.q: Your client wrote notes about their case using a consumer chatbot, on their own. The other side asks for them in discovery. What is the main risk?
opts: None, because all AI chats are privileged
Only the AI company can be asked for them
A court may find they are not privileged or work product, as the court did in United States v. Heppner
Chatbots delete everything after a day
scenario.feedback: In Heppner, a federal judge held that a defendant's own AI chats were not privileged or work product. Warn clients early.

modules.title: What's next in AI
modules.desc: AI agents that carry out tasks, AI that reads scans and transcribes speech, and how to keep up with the rules.
recap: AI agents carry out tasks with many steps, so your duty to supervise covers their work.
AI can read scans and transcribe speech. Check recording laws and treat transcripts as drafts.
Keep up by knowing your bar's guidance, your courts' rules and your employer's policy.

scenario.q: An AI agent at your firm drafted a settlement offer and was about to email it to opposing counsel on its own. What safeguard was missing?
opts: A rule that a person approves anything sent to a client, a court or the other side
A faster AI model
A longer prompt
Nothing was missing
scenario.feedback: Agents need firm limits. A person should approve anything sent outside the firm, filed or paid.

modules.title: How AI works inside
modules.desc: An extra module for technical readers and legal technologists. Covers tokens, training, how legal AI tools are built, agents and testing.
recap: Models read and write tokens, only see what fits in the context window, and pick each token by chance.
Training gives a model knowledge up to a cutoff date. Feedback training makes it helpful, and sometimes too eager to answer.
Most legal AI tools combine a model with search over real legal sources. Test them on your own kind of work.

scenario.q: A vendor says its legal research tool "cannot hallucinate because it uses RAG." What is the best response?
opts: Accept the claim
Ask the tool whether the claim is true
Turn off the retrieval feature
Ask for the vendor's test results and run your own test set, because retrieval reduces errors but does not remove them
scenario.feedback: Looking up real sources first helps, but the Stanford study found leading legal tools still gave false or misleading answers 17 to 33 percent of the time.

modules.title: Your professional duties
modules.desc: How the ethics rules apply to AI: competence, confidentiality and privilege, courts and candor, and checking AI research.
recap: ABA Formal Opinion 512 and state bar guidance apply the existing ethics rules to AI. Check your own state's rules.
Get informed consent when required before putting client information into an AI tool, and read the tool's terms.
Check the court's local rules and the judge's standing orders on AI before every filing.
Find, read and check every authority yourself. Never ask the AI to check itself.

scenario.q: After filing a brief, you find that one case you cited does not say what you claimed. What should you do?
opts: Wait to see if anyone notices
Promptly correct the record with the court
Blame the AI tool in a footnote
Delete the case from your own copy
scenario.feedback: The duty of candor requires correcting false statements made to a court. Courts have been harsher on lawyers who hid mistakes than on those who fixed them.

modules.title: Legal AI tools and AI law
modules.desc: The main kinds of legal AI tools, how to choose one, and the laws that regulate AI.
recap: Legal AI tools ground answers in real sources and protect data better, but they still make mistakes.
Choose a tool for a specific task, get data promises in the contract and test it on your own work.
The EU AI Act sorts AI by risk. U.S. rules come from existing laws, states, cities, courts and bars.

scenario.q: Your firm wants to buy a legal AI drafting tool. What should come first?
opts: Buy the most popular tool
Let each lawyer choose a different tool
Choose a specific task, check the vendor's data terms and run a trial on work like your own
Ask the tool's chatbot for a discount
scenario.feedback: A specific task, written data promises and your own trial are the best evidence that a tool will help.

modules.title: AI by practice area
modules.desc: How AI shows up in litigation and discovery, in contracts and deals, and on in-house legal teams.
recap: Litigators can use AI for review, summaries and drafts, but must check every citation and quote and follow court rules on AI.
Transactional lawyers can speed up contract review, but should check a sample by hand and decide the hard calls themselves.
In-house teams use AI and also set the company's AI rules, including for high-risk uses such as hiring.

scenario.q: You want to load documents produced under a protective order into an AI review tool. What do you check first?
opts: Whether the protective order allows it, and whether the tool is approved and keeps the data secure
Whether the tool is fast
Whether opposing counsel uses AI
Nothing, because review tools are always allowed
scenario.feedback: A protective order limits how produced documents may be used and shared. Check it before loading the documents into any tool.

questions.q: How often do you use AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini?
opts: Never, or I'm not sure if I have
I've tried one a few times
Every week
Every day, or I build things with them
phrase: have tried AI a few times

questions.q: How much do you know about technology?
opts: Not much. I use the basics on my computer and phone.
I'm comfortable with computers and apps.
I have some technical skills, like spreadsheet formulas or a little coding.
A lot. I write code or work in IT, data or engineering.

questions.q: What do you most want from this course?
opts: To understand what AI is and why it matters for law
To use AI well in law school or while studying law
To use AI safely in legal practice
To understand how legal AI tools work, or help choose and build them
phrase: understand what AI is and why it matters for law
use AI well while studying law
use AI safely in legal practice
understand how legal AI tools work

questions.q: How much time do you usually have when you sit down to learn?
opts: About 10 minutes
About 20 minutes
45 minutes or more

glossary.def: Computer systems that do jobs that usually need human thinking, like understanding speech, making choices or writing text.
The trained AI system inside an app that does the work. ChatGPT is an app. The GPT models are the models inside it.
A way of building AI where the computer learns from examples. Nobody writes all its rules by hand. More good examples usually make it better.
A strong kind of machine learning. It uses neural networks with many layers to find complicated patterns.
Layers of simple math, loosely inspired by the brain. Together they turn an input, like a photo, into an output, like the word "cat."
An AI trained on a huge amount of text. It can write, sum up, translate and hold conversations. Chatbots run on these models.
An app you can talk to in everyday language, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot.
AI that makes new things, such as text, pictures, sound, video or code. Older AI mostly sorted or checked things that already existed.
The message or instructions you give an AI. Clear, detailed prompts with some background get better results.
When an AI states something false as if it were true, such as a made-up case, a wrong citation or an invented quote.
The examples an AI learns from. How good and how varied they are shapes what the AI knows and how fair it is.
How an AI learns from its training data. It guesses, checks the answer and adjusts itself, millions of times.
The numbers inside a model that store what it learned. Training adjusts them. Large models have billions of them.
A chunk of text, about a word or part of a word. Language models read and write tokens. Usage limits are often counted in tokens.
How much text an AI can consider at once, including your conversation and any documents. A bigger window can handle longer material.
A model, or a setting in a chatbot, that works through a problem step by step before it answers. It is slower and better at hard tasks. Also called a reasoning model.
AI that works with several kinds of information, such as text, pictures, sound and video, often at the same time.
An AI that takes actions to reach a goal. It might browse the web, fill in forms or write code, as well as reply with text.
The kind of AI behind most picture and video tools. It starts with random static and cleans it up into a picture that matches your description.
The design behind almost all modern language models. Google researchers introduced it in 2017. It lets a model compare every word with every other word.
Extra training for a model that already exists, using special examples. It makes the model better at one task or style.
A model whose trained settings are published, so anyone can download, run and change it. Examples are Meta's Llama and models from Mistral and DeepSeek. Also called an open-weight model.
A method where the AI first looks up useful documents and then writes its answer from them. It cuts down on made-up facts.
A setting that controls how predictable an AI's answers are. A low setting gives steady answers. A high setting gives more varied and surprising ones.
When an AI gives unfair results for some groups of people. It usually happens because the training data was one-sided.
A realistic fake photo, video or voice recording of a real person, made with AI. Deepfakes raise new questions about evidence.
A label attached to a file that records whether and how AI was used to make or change it. Some cameras, apps and websites show it.
An AI that could do any thinking task as well as a person. It does not exist yet, and experts disagree about whether or when it will.
A set of rules that lets one program ask another program for something. Apps send requests to an AI model's API and get replies back.
Instructions given to a model before the conversation starts. They set its role, its tone and its rules.
A list of numbers that stands for the meaning of a piece of text. It lets a computer quickly find texts with similar meanings.
Training a model to give the kinds of answers that people rated as better.
When a model asks an app to run a tool, such as a search or a calculator, and then uses the result in its answer. Also called function calling.
An open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and information in one standard way.
A set of test examples used to measure how well an AI system works. Teams run it again after every change. Also called evals.
Hidden or harmful instructions inside a document, email or web page. They try to make an AI do something it shouldn't.
The date a model's training data ends. The model knows nothing after that date unless it searches the web or you give it documents.
A rule of evidence that keeps private communications between a client and lawyer, made to get legal advice, out of court. Sharing them with outsiders can waive it.
A lawyer's ethical duty to protect all information about a client's matter. That covers far more than privileged communications.
Materials prepared by or for a lawyer in anticipation of a lawsuit. They are usually protected from the other side in discovery.
A client's agreement after the lawyer has explained the risks and the other options. Some AI uses need it.
Using machine learning to sort documents in a lawsuit by how likely they are to be relevant. Also called predictive coding.
Finding, collecting and reviewing electronic information, such as emails and files, for a lawsuit.
A service, such as Shepard's or KeyCite, that shows whether a case or statute is still good law and which later cases cite it.
A judge's own rules for every case before that judge. Some cover how lawyers may use AI.
The federal court rule that makes a lawyer's signature on a filing a promise that its legal arguments are supported by the law after a reasonable inquiry.
A lawyer's duty not to make false statements of law or fact to a court, and to correct them if made.
Barriers inside a firm that keep people working on one matter from seeing information about another, to avoid conflicts.
The American Bar Association's July 2024 ethics opinion on lawyers' use of generative AI. It covers competence, confidentiality, communication, candor, supervision and fees.
The European Union's law on AI. It sorts AI systems by risk, with the strictest duties for high-risk uses such as hiring and credit.
A test that compares an AI tool's results across groups of people, such as by sex and race, to find unfair differences.
